items.text: Madagascar faces political turmoil as President Andry Rajoelina goes into hiding after an assassination attempt. Weeks of nationwide protests, mainly led by young demonstrators called ‘Gen Z Mada,’ demanded his resignation due to issues like unemployment, corruption, and the high cost of living. The protests escalated when an elite army unit joined, intensifying pressure on the president. Rajoelina dissolved the national assembly and dismissed his government, appointing only a few ministers. In a Facebook broadcast, he confirmed he left the country for safety but didn’t reveal his location, leaving citizens uncertain about who governs the country. Opposition leaders now aim to impeach him, but they need to convince ruling party MPs to proceed. The unrest stems from long-standing problems that the president failed to resolve over his years in power. People demanded better access to basic services, but the movement expanded to call for leadership change. The political future remains uncertain as the opposition seeks to organize elections and a transitional government . Difficult words: turmoil (a situation with a lot of confusion, problems, or chaos), elite (a small, powerful, or important group of people), impeach (to formally accuse a leader of wrongdoing), transitional government (a temporary government that rules until a new official government is ready). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In Madagascar, President Andry Rajoelina hides after people tried to harm him. Many young protesters, called ‘Gen Z Mada,’ asked him to resign because of unemployment, corruption, and high living costs. The protests grew when some soldiers joined them. Rajoelina ended the national assembly and fired most of his government. He spoke on Facebook but didn’t say where he was. People don’t know who leads the country now. Opposition groups try to convince members of the ruling party to remove him. People first want better water and electricity, but now they want the president to leave. They are worried about the future of the country and hope for a new government and elections soon. Difficult words: resign (to leave a job or position), national assembly (a group of people who make laws for a country), convince (to make someone believe or agree with you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Madagascar, people protest against President Andry Rajoelina. Many young people want him to leave. Some soldiers help the protesters. The president hides in a safe place. He stops the national assembly and fires some workers. People do not know who the leader is now. People want better water and electricity. They want a new leader. People hope that they can vote soon and have a new government. Everyone is worried about what will happen next. Difficult words: hide (to go somewhere where other people cannot see you), national assembly (a group of people who make laws for a country), fire (to make someone leave their job). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Researchers at Flinders University in Australia have discovered that new shark-bite-resistant wetsuits can significantly reduce injuries during shark attacks. These suits are made from materials containing strong fibers such as Kevlar and polyethylene, which help protect against deep cuts and blood loss. Although the suits cannot completely prevent internal injuries, they can lower the number and severity of wounds, giving victims more time to receive emergency help. Tests were done using white and tiger sharks, and the results showed that these new materials performed much better than regular neoprene. Researchers were surprised by how much damage was reduced. Shark attacks are rare, but they can be fatal , so any improvement in protection is important. Traditional chain mail suits used for diving are too heavy and inflexible for surfers, so the goal now is to make these new materials more flexible while keeping them strong enough to save lives. Difficult words: Kevlar (a strong synthetic fiber), fatal (causing death), chain mail (small metal rings linked together). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Scientists at Flinders University in Australia are testing new wetsuits that help protect people from shark bites . These wetsuits use very strong materials, which make the injuries smaller and help people lose less blood. Shark attacks don’t happen often, but they can kill people. The suits cannot stop all injuries, but they can make shark bites less dangerous. The scientists try the suits with white and tiger sharks. They see that the new materials work better than normal wetsuits. Old metal suits are too heavy and hard to move in, so the team wants to make new suits that are softer and easier for surfers to use, but still very strong. Difficult words: wetsuit (a tight piece of clothing that people wear in water to keep warm and protect their body), bit e (to use your teeth to cut or injure), injury (hurt to the body). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Australia, experts at Flinders University test new wetsuits for people in the sea. These suits help when a shark bites . Shark bites do not happen many times, but they are very bad when they do. The new suit has very strong fabric . It helps the person have smaller cuts and lose less blood. The people test the suits with white sharks and tiger sharks. The new suit is better than the normal one. Old metal suits are too big and hard to move in. The new one is lighter and easier for surfers to use. It helps them stay safe in the water. Difficult words: wetsuit (a piece of clothing which people wear in water, usually surfers or divers), bite (to use the teeth to cut or injure), fabric (cloth or material for clothes). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Global spending on AI is increasing rapidly, reaching 330 billion dollars in 2025 and possibly 2 trillion dollars by 2030. Tech giants are investing huge amounts in chips, data centers, and electricity grids, creating what experts call an AI supercycle. Some analysts worry that this massive investment might hide weaknesses in the economy. Without AI-related spending, the US could already be in a recession . Others see AI as the next industrial revolution, bringing productivity and innovation. However, there are financial risks: many companies borrow money to fund expansion, which could cause problems if profits fall. Another concern is inequality . The AI boom benefits investors and homeowners, while many workers struggle with slow wage growth and fewer job opportunities. Around 60% of jobs could change or disappear because of automation . Still, many believe AI will create new industries and support future economic growth. Difficult words: recession (a time when a country’s economy is not doing well, people earn less, and many lose jobs), inequality (an unfair difference between groups of people), automation (using machines to do work instead of people). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

AI spending is growing very fast. By 2030, it could reach 2 trillion dollars each year. Big companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft are building new computer systems and data centers. Some people worry that this spending hides economic problems. They think the economy looks strong only because of AI money. Others believe AI will help the economy grow and make work faster. Still, there are risks. If companies borrow too much money and profits fall, it could hurt the economy. Also, not everyone benefits from AI. Rich people and big companies earn more, but many workers earn less or lose jobs. Experts say 60% of jobs could change because of AI. Difficult words: hide (to keep something secret or make it difficult to see), economy (system of money and work in a country), benefits (to get something good or helpful from something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

People spend a lot of money on AI. Big companies use it to make new computers and tools . This can help businesses and make work faster. Some people think that this is good. Others worry that it can make problems. Companies sometimes take money from banks. If they cannot pay, they have trouble . Some people get more money from AI, but others do not. Some people think that it is not fair. Also, many workers are afraid that they can lose their jobs. Still, some people think that AI can create new jobs and help the world grow in the future . Difficult words: tool (something you use to do a job or task), trouble (a problem), future (the time that will come after now). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Have you wondered why US school buses are yellow? In the past, school transportation had no rules, and children walked or rode horse-drawn wagons to school. Later, some districts instilled patriotism with red, white, and blue buses, but the colors changed with Frank Cyr. Cyr was a professor at Columbia University, and in 1939, he organized a conference on the school bus. Teachers, transportation experts, engineers, and paint specialists wrote with 42 pages of school bus regulations. They decided to use yellow because black letters were easy to see on a yellow background, and yellow stood out in bad weather. The color is now officially known as national school bus glossy yellow. Every day in the US, 480,000 school buses drive children to school. The federal law doesn’t require all buses to be yellow; however, safety experts recommend it. Difficult words: instill (to put an idea or attitude in a person’s mind), patriotism (the feeling that you are proud of your country more than any others), glossy (shiny). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Over time, most school buses in the US became the same yellow color. In the past, many children walked or used horses to go to school. Later, red, white, and blue buses took children to support patriotism . In 1939, a professor at Columbia University met with teachers, engineers, and other experts. They wrote a document of 42 pages that was about school buses. Experts recommended to make the school buses yellow because black letters on yellow can be seen easily. Also, yellow buses were more visible in bad weather. The yellow color got its own name, and although no law says that school buses must be yellow, most of the 480,000 school US buses are yellow. Difficult words: patriotism (the feeling that you love your country, and you are very proud of it), recommend (to say what someone should do), visible (something that people can see). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

480,000 school buses are in the US. They take children to school every day. Most of them are yellow. In 1939, a university professor meets with teachers, engineers , and other experts. They discuss school buses to make them safer. Experts say that the yellow color is the best. You can easily see black letters on it. When the weather is bad, people can see yellow easily. No US law says that school buses must be yellow. Many people believe that yellow is the safest color. Now, most buses are yellow. The color even has its own name. Difficult words: engineer (a person who designs and builds machines, buildings, and so on), letter (the symbol of an alphabet, for example, a, b, c, and so on), law (the rules of a country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

AI-generated short videos, often called AI slop, are flooding the internet, replacing real and authentic content. These clips, usually around eight seconds long, are designed to trigger emotions before viewers can think critically. Because they are short, they can be made quickly and shared widely, which makes them powerful tools for spreading misinformation. Many of these videos show fake events, such as disasters or celebrity news, that look convincing at first glance. Experts explain that creating longer AI videos requires huge computing power, which is why most stay short. There are ways to spot AI videos: they often have strange movements, gibberish text, and no camera motion. Some companies, like Google, are trying to mark AI content with invisible watermarks, but they are not visible to users. Viewers must stay alert, check other sources, and avoid sharing suspicious content to protect themselves from digital deception . Difficult words: authentic (real), convincing (making you believe that something is true or real), gibberish (nonsense text or speech), deception (making someone believe something false). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Short videos made by AI, called AI slop, are everywhere online. They often last about eight seconds and can easily trick people. These videos look real but show fake news, disasters, or events. They spread fast because people share them quickly. Experts say making longer AI videos needs a lot of computer power. We can find fake clips by watching for signs like strange hand shapes, nonsense words, or no camera movement. Some companies, such as Google, try to mark AI videos with secret watermarks , but it is hard to see them. People must stay careful, check other pages before believing something, and stop sharing videos that look weird. Difficult words: trick (to make someone believe something that is not true), nonsense (something that has no meaning or sense), watermark (a mark on an image or video that shows who owns it or that it is official). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

There are many short videos on the internet. AI makes many of them. People call them AI slop. These videos are very short, about eight seconds long. They can show fake things and make people feel sad or angry. Some look real, but they are not. AI videos are easy to make and share. It is hard to know which videos are true. You can look for signs : strange hands, words that do not make sense , or no camera moves. Always check other pages or real news before you believe or share. Think first and do not help spread fake videos. Difficult words: sign (something what tells or shows that something is happening), sense (understanding something), spread (to move or pass from one place to another). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A new study discovered that regular soda drinking leads to an increased risk for many causes of death. The study surveyed more than 450,000 people in 10 European countries from 1992 to 2000. The study discovered that people who drank two or more glasses of soda a day had a higher chance of dying from certain diseases than people who drank less than one glass of soda a day. Soda sweetened with sugar is linked to more digestive diseases, and soda sweetened with artificial sugar is linked to more circulatory diseases. Also, drinking any soda excessively is linked to Parkinson’s disease. Researchers said that drinking a lot of soda suggests that you might have an unhealthy lifestyle, but the results were the same whether you were skinny, overweight, smoked, or did not smoke cigarettes. Difficult words: soda (sweet drinks like Coca-Cola, Sprite, etc.), digestive (related to digestion in the body – when your body takes in what you eat or drink), circulatory (related to the circulation of blood), Parkinson’s (a disease that affects the brain and eventually kills a person). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A new study found that drinking soda leads to a greater risk for many causes of death. The study surveyed over 450,000 people in 10 European countries from 1992 to 2000. The study found that people who drank two or more glasses of soda a day had higher chances of dying from certain diseases, and people who drank less than one glass of soda a day had less chances. Experts said that drinking a lot of soda shows that you can have an unhealthy lifestyle. However, the study’s results were the same whether you were skinny, overweight, smoked, or did not smoke cigarettes. Difficult words: soda (sweet drinks like Coca-Cola, Sprite, etc.), survey (ask many people the same kind of questions to get some information). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

An organization does a study . Experts talk to over 450,000 people in 10 European countries. They do this from 1992 to 2000. Their study finds that drinking a lot of soda is very bad for people’s health. The study finds that it is bad to drink more than two glasses of soda a day. The soda can lead to diseases which can kill people. Experts say that it is unhealthy to drink a lot of soda for anyone. You can be skinny. You can be a non-smoker. Soda can still lead to some diseases. Difficult words: soda (sweet drinks like coca cola, sprite, etc.), study (when experts try to learn something by doing work and get information), disease (a very bad sickness). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Denmark, long known as a pioneer in clean energy, is now developing green methanol — a low-carbon fuel made using renewable power. This new fuel can power ships and industries and serve as an ingredient for plastics, paint, and glue. The world’s first commercial-scale green methanol plant has started operation in southern Denmark. Using electricity from a large solar farm, the facility produces hydrogen by splitting water and combines it with biogenic CO₂ from biogas created using animal waste. This process results in methanol that has a much smaller carbon footprint than traditional, fossil-fuel-based methanol. Companies like Maersk, Lego, and Novo Nordisk are already using it in shipping, toy production, and medicine. Although producing green methanol is still expensive and energy-intensive, Denmark plans to expand production and reduce costs. The project represents a milestone in the global effort to make transport and industry more sustainable. Difficult words: pioneer (a person or company who starts something new), biogenic (made from living things), milestone (an important event or step). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Denmark is one of the first countries to make green methanol, a new kind of clean fuel . This fuel can power ships, planes, and factories, and we can use it to make plastics, paint, and glue. The new factory in the south of Denmark uses solar energy to make hydrogen from water. Then, it mixes the hydrogen with CO₂ from animal waste to make green methanol. Big companies like Maersk and Lego already use it in their work. Making this fuel costs more money than normal fuel, but Denmark wants to make more of it in the future. It is a big step for cleaner transport and for the world’s fight against climate change. Difficult words: fuel (something that gives energy), waste (things we no longer need). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Denmark makes new green fuel to help the planet. This fuel can help ships, planes, and cars. It can also help make things like plastic and paint . The new factory in Denmark uses power from the sun. It takes water and makes a gas called hydrogen . Then, it mixes it with another gas to make green methanol. This new fuel is better for our planet because it is not so bad for the air. Big companies, like Maersk and Lego, want to use it. Now it costs a lot, but Denmark wants to make more soon. This new fuel can make our world cleaner and safer. Difficult words: fuel (something what gives energy), paint (a colored substance which we put on walls, wood, or other things to make them look nice), hydrogen (a light gas from water). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A ceasefire between Israel and Hamas has started in Gaza, allowing many Palestinians to return to their destroyed homes after months of fighting. Around 200,000 people are walking back through ruined towns while Israeli forces still hold half of the territory. Under the agreement, Hamas must release 20 Israeli hostages and the bodies of 28 others, while Israel will free 250 Palestinian prisoners and more than 1,700 detainees from Gaza. Both sides have 72 hours to complete these steps. This ceasefire is only the first stage of a wider plan that includes rebuilding Gaza and deciding who will govern it. Many details remain unclear, and the future of the region depends on how the sides follow the terms. Israeli families of former hostages expressed relief and hope for peace, though international observers warn that major challenges remain before lasting stability can be achieved. Difficult words: hostage (a person kept by someone to make others do what they want), detainee (someone kept in prison), stability (a state of peace without a sudden change). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The fighting between Israel and Hamas stopped after a new ceasefire began in Gaza. Thousands of Palestinians are walking back to their homes, but many towns are broken and full of ruins . Israel still controls part of Gaza. According to the deal, Hamas must let 20 Israeli hostages go and return 28 bodies. In return, Israel must free 250 prisoners and 1,700 people taken during the war. This deal is only the first part of a bigger plan to rebuild Gaza and decide who will lead it. People in Israel and Gaza hope for peace, but there are still many problems. Officials must solve them before life can return to normal. Difficult words: ceasefire (time when a war stops), ruin (what remains of a broken building), hostage (a person who is not free and who must do what somebody else says). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The war between Israel and Hamas stops for now. There is a ceasefire . People in Gaza can go home again. Many houses are gone. The streets are full of broken things. Israeli soldiers stay in part of Gaza. Hamas must give 20 Israeli people back and 28 bodies. Israel must let 250 Palestinians and 1,700 other people go from jail . This is only the start of a plan. Later, people will fix the houses and talk about who will lead Gaza. Families in Israel and Gaza feel happy but also scared . They hope that the fighting does not start again. Difficult words: ceasefire (time when a war stops), jail (a place for people who break the law), scared (afraid). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The consulting firm Deloitte used AI to help prepare a government report for Australia’s Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. The report cost 440,000 dollars but contained serious errors, including fake legal quotes and references that AI had invented. This happened because AI sometimes “ hallucinates ”. It creates false information to fill gaps. The mistakes were later discovered by an academic and made public. Although Deloitte corrected some details and offered a partial refund, the situation caused major embarrassment for both the company and the government. Experts say this incident shows the risks of using AI without proper human checking. Many businesses use AI, often without managers realizing how much, which makes accuracy a growing concern. The case has become a wake-up call for organizations to use technology responsibly and verify results carefully before presenting them as facts. Difficult words: hallucinate (to imagine things that are not real), academic (a person who teaches or studies at a university), wake-up call (something that makes people notice a big problem and start to act). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The consulting company Deloitte made a report for the Australian government using AI. The report cost 440,000 dollars, but it had big mistakes. The computer wrote fake names and wrong quotes from judges. AI sometimes makes up information when it doesn’t know the answer. Later, a teacher found these mistakes and told the media about them. Deloitte changed some parts of the report and gave some money back to the government. The company and the department felt embarrassed . Many people in offices now use AI, but not everyone tells their boss. This story shows that people must check AI work carefully. AI can help, but it can also make big errors if people don’t watch what it does. Difficult words: consulting company (a business that gives expert advice to other businesses or the government), quote (the exact words that someone said or wrote), embarrassed (feeling bad or shy because of a mistake or something awkward). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A big company called Deloitte makes a report for the Australian government . It uses AI to help write it. The report has many mistakes and wrong names. The computer makes fake quotes and stories which are not real. A teacher finds the mistakes and tells the news. The company says sorry and gives some money back. The government feels angry and surprised. Now, many people talk about this problem. Many workers use AI every day in their jobs. AI can write fast, but sometimes it makes big mistakes. People must check the AI work carefully. AI can help, but it is not always right or smart. Difficult words: government (the group of people who lead and make rules for a country), mistake (something what is not correct), quote (what someone says or writes). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Charlotte Chopin, a 102-year-old yoga teacher from France, has been teaching for more than forty years. She started yoga at fifty and soon began leading classes in her small village, Léré. Her studio is located in an old police station, and she teaches a few loyal students each week. Despite her age, she still moves with grace and energy, inspiring others with her strength and discipline. Charlotte became famous after appearing on a talent show at ninety-nine, where her calmness and control impressed the audience. She later received recognition from India for promoting yoga and healthy living. However, she stays humble and says her long life is mostly due to good luck, daily movement, and friendship. Her days are simple: coffee and toast for breakfast, some outdoor time, and yoga. She believes that staying active, grateful, and connected helps her live happily and age well. Difficult words: grace (smooth and beautiful movement), recognition (public respect or praise), humble (not proud; thinking you are not more important than other people). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Charlotte Chopin is 102 years old and lives in a small village in France. She started yoga when she was fifty and soon started to teach other people. Her studio is in an old police building, and she gives lessons to a few women every week. She is strong and calm, and her students like her very much. At ninety-nine, Charlotte went on a TV show and became famous for her yoga poses . Later, India gave her an award for helping people know more about yoga. She says she just feels lucky and happy to do what she loves. Every day she eats breakfast, goes outside, and does yoga. She believes that good friends, a simple life, and movement keep her healthy and happy. Difficult words: studio (a place to teach or do an activity), pose (a position of your body, often for exercise, yoga, or a photo), award (something you get for good work). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Charlotte Chopin is 102 years old. She lives in a small village in France. She does yoga and teaches other people. She starts yoga when she is fifty. Her yoga room is in an old police station. She has some students. They like her classes very much. Charlotte is strong and happy. She likes yoga and her friends. When she is ninety-nine, she goes on TV. Many people see her and clap . India gives her a special gift for teaching people about yoga. Every day, Charlotte eats toast and drinks coffee. She goes outside and moves her body. She says that yoga helps her feel good and live a long life. Difficult words: village (a place where people live, smaller than a town), clap (to hit your hands together to show you like something or to make a sound). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

This is an inspirational story for people who want to learn English. This could be your story too. I am on holiday abroad. My friends and I have just sat down in a beautiful restaurant with a view of the sea. The staff speak only English. Luckily, our friend Peter knows English, so we feel safe. We can rely on him to order our food. Suddenly, Peter’s phone rings. He apologizes and says he has to deal with something urgent . He tells us, “Please order one beer and a steak with baked potatoes for me.” After he leaves, the waiter comes over, smiles, and hands us the menus. Then he asks in English what we would like to drink. It is a quiet moment. We look at each other. After all, no one except Peter speaks English but I know that this is my moment. I smile, look at the waiter, and say, “I’ll have a glass of wine and some water, please.” Then I ask each friend what they want and tell the waiter their orders. When the waiter leaves, there is silence . My friends look at me in disbelief. They can’t understand what just happened. Then one friend asks, “When did you learn English?” I smile and answer, “I started learning not long ago. I use LangoPlay. It’s a game where you learn English through a story. I play every day and learn a few new words each time. It really works.” There is a short pause, and then another friend says, “Can you show me? Maybe I will try it too.” I nod , “Sure. LangoPlay is simple. You can start for free and play anytime at www.langoplay.com .” Difficult words: urgent (very important to do now), silence (a quiet moment), nod (to move your head down and up).

I play every day and learn some new words each time. It really helps.” There is a short pause. Then another friend says, “Can you show me? Maybe I will try it too.” I say, “Of course. LangoPlay is easy. You can start for free and play anytime at www.langoplay.com .” Difficult words: trust (to believe), surprised (a little shocked).

The waiters in the restaurant speak English. Our friend Peter speaks English too. He can order food for us. At one moment, Peter’s phone rings. You can start for free. You can play at www.langoplay.com .” Difficult words: order (to say what you want at a restaurant), rings (when a phone makes a sound), important (when something is important, you must do it).

The Nobel Prize in Physics 2025 is awarded to John Clarke, Michel Devoret, and John Martinis for their research in quantum mechanics, which allows tiny particles to behave in unusual ways and lays the foundation for modern quantum computers. Their discoveries show how the strange properties of the quantum world can be used on a larger, human scale. These computers can perform calculations much faster than conventional machines and solve problems in finance, logistics, and cryptography that normal computers struggle with. The prize was announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden. The three scientists will share a total of 11 million Swedish kronor. Their research, which began decades ago, connects basic science with technological applications. It has helped develop electron tunneling devices and microchips, forming the basis for today’s quantum computing industry. Experts believe this work will continue to shape technology and expand our understanding of quantum mechanics in practical ways. Difficult words: quantum mechanics (a branch of science that studies very tiny things like atoms and particles, and how they behave in unusual ways), property (a characteristic or feature of something, describing how it behaves or looks), cryptography (the science or practice of making secret codes to protect information). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Three scientists — John Clarke, Michel Devoret, and John Martinis — win the Nobel Prize in Physics for their work in quantum mechanics. They discovered how very small particles can behave in strange ways, and their work helps build quantum computers, which can calculate faster than normal computers. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Sweden announced the winners, who will share 11 million Swedish kronor. Their research started decades ago, but it is very important today. It helps scientists and companies create new technology, like better computers and new ways to solve difficult problems. Many banks and industries now use ideas from their work. Difficult words: quantum mechanics (a science which studies very small things and how they behave in unusual ways), particle (a very small piece of matter), quantum computer (a computer that uses quantum mechanics to process information much faster than other computers). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Three scientists — John Clarke, Michel Devoret, and John Martinis — win the Nobel Prize in Physics. They study quantum mechanics, a science about very small things like atoms. Their work helps people make quantum computers, which can do some jobs faster than normal computers. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Sweden gives the prize. The scientists share 11 million Swedish kronor for their great work. Their ideas start many years ago but are very important today. They help people build new technology and change how we live and work. Difficult words: quantum mechanics (science which studies very small things and how they behave in unusual ways), quantum computer (a computer that uses quantum mechanics to process information much faster than other computers), prize (an award). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Andrej Babiš, a billionaire businessman and former Czech prime minister, has led his political movement ANO (meaning “Yes”) to victory in the Czech parliamentary elections, winning 34.6% of the vote. His success ends the rule of Prime Minister Petr Fiala’s pro-Western coalition, which received 23.3%. To form a new government, Babiš will need to cooperate with another party, possibly the Freedom and Direct Democracy group or the Motorists for Themselves party. Known for his critical stance toward the European Union, Babiš has joined Hungarian and Slovak leaders in opposing EU sanctions on Russia and limiting military aid to Ukraine. He has also expressed doubts about increasing defence spending under NATO commitments. Babiš’s campaign focused on domestic concerns such as cheaper energy, higher pensions, and prioritising Czech interests over foreign affairs. His victory signals a shift in Czech politics toward more nationalist and Eurosceptic policies. Difficult words: prioritise (to decide what is most important and do that first), signal (to show or give a sign that something is happening), shift (a change in direction or attitude). Andrej Babiš, a rich businessman and former leader of the Czech Republic, won the national elections with his party ANO. His group got about 34.6% of the votes, more than the current prime minister Petr Fiala’s team. Babiš now needs another party to help him form a government. He may work with smaller parties that agree with him. Babiš often speaks against the European Union and doesn’t support giving weapons to Ukraine. He wants to spend less money on defence and focus more on his own country. During his campaign , he promised cheaper energy and better pensions for people in Czechia. Many voters liked his idea of putting Czech citizens first. Difficult words: defence (protection of a country), campaign (planned actions to reach a goal, especially in politics or business), citizen (a person who belongs to a country and has rights there). Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party has chosen Sanae Takaichi as its new leader, putting her on track to become Japan’s first female prime minister. Takaichi aims to revive her struggling party while an anti-immigration movement gains support. She has been active in politics since 1993 and has held many government roles. She is known for her firm stance on traditional family values. Despite being a woman, she opposes feminist ideas such as separate family names or women succeeding to the imperial throne. Her leadership comes at a difficult time for the party, which has lost public trust due to corruption scandals and rising prices. Internationally, her close ties to nationalist groups and visits to controversial war memorials have caused tension with China and South Korea. As she prepares for office, Japan and the world are watching to see whether she maintains her hardline policies or adopts a softer approach. Difficult words: on track (likely to achieve something or reach a goal soon), stance (an opinion or position on an issue), hardline (having very strict and strong opinions and not wanting to change them). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Difficult words: traditional (connected with old customs or ideas), scandal (an event which shocks people because it is wrong or dishonest), feminist (supporting the same rights and rules for women and men). Some Americans check their smartphones 96 times a day, or once every 10 minutes. Screen time additionally creates digital eye strain and can damage eye parts and the ability to focus . Children are getting more screen time due to the pandemic. Children’s screen time went from 6 hours to 13 hours a day. Some studies show that too much screen time leads to lower language and thinking test scores and the thinning of the brain’s cortex , where we do critical thinking and reasoning. The screens also impact their sleep, and sleep is important to the brain’s development and memory. Blue light from screens lowers a brain chemical called melatonin; melatonin helps you go to sleep. The screens then keep children more awake at night. Difficult words: digital eye strain (when your eyes get tired from looking at screens too much), focus (to see clearly with both of your eyes), cortex (the front of the brain). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Some Americans look at their smartphones and other screens, such as computers or TVs for more than 8 hours a day. Many people sleep less than 8 hours per night. Unfortunately, screen time can tire or hurt your eyes and brain. Due to COVID, children are getting more screen time. Some studies show that too much screen time can lower their language and thinking test scores and thin the brain’s cortex . The cortex is where people solve problems or make arguments. The screens are also negative for their sleep, and sleep is important to their brain’s growth. The screens make a blue light which tells their brain to delay sleep. The blue light then keeps children more alert at night when they should sleep. Difficult words: thin (to get smaller), cortex (the front of the brain), delay (to wait). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Some Americans look at screens more than 8 hours a day. Many people sleep less than 8 hours a night. Unfortunately , screen time can hurt your eyes and brain. Ghana has suspended all boxing events after two professional fighters died this year. The government announced a three-month ban to create stronger regulations for the sport. A new committee will decide how to make boxing safer before athletes can compete again. The first death occurred in March when Nigerian boxer Gabriel Olanrewaju collapsed during a fight in Accra. The second happened just weeks ago, when Ghanaian boxer Ernest Akushey died 11 days after his match. Authorities said the suspension is necessary to protect lives and rebuild trust in the sport. They also plan a five-year strategy to improve safety and bring Ghanaian boxing up to international standards. Boxing is one of Ghana’s most loved sports, with famous champions like Azumah Nelson, but recent tragedies have forced the nation to rethink how it is managed and monitored. Difficult words: suspend (to stop something for some time), regulation (a rule or law that controls an activity). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Ghana stopped all boxing after two boxers died this year. The government said there will be no fights for at least three months while a new team makes rules to keep boxers safe. They also want to make new long-term plans for better training and control . Boxing is very popular in Ghana and gave the country famous champions , but now many people want to make sure it is safe for everyone. Difficult words: long-term (something that lasts for a long time or happens over many years), control (to manage, guide, or direct something so it works the way you want), champion (a person who wins a competition or is the best at a sport or activity). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Zohra Zarougui, a Tunisian artist, paints on water using an ancient technique of marbling called Ebru. This art is not taught in Tunisia, so Zarougui had to travel and study abroad. She got a master’s degree, and after years of research and experimentation, she returned to Tunisia. The artist creates pieces from patterns from old cities in the Arab world. She sprinkles brightly colored dyes into pans of oily water and then transfers the patterns onto a piece of paper canvas. According to Zarougui, it takes years of studying to be able to bring out the history of this art and its techniques and methods. Her experience lasted several years outside the country, and it took a lot of courage and sacrifice . The art of Ebru first appeared and evolved in the 15th century in Persia and Ottoman Turkey. Some of the methods use colors which float on the top of a bath of liquid mucilage . Difficult words: dye (a substance that people use to change the color of clothes, hair, and so on), sacrifice (to give up something that you like or want to keep to get something else or help someone), mucilage (a thick gooey substance that’ comes from plants and some microorganisms). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Zohra Zarougui is a Tunisian artist who uses a very old style of painting called Ebru. Ebru is from the 15th century, and it comes from old Iran, Persia, and old Turkey, Ottoman Turkey. Since that time, it moved to more countries, for example, India or China, where artists used different colors and ways to make it. Zarougui uses a pan of oily water, and she adds dyes to make beautifully colored patterns . She then takes a piece of paper or canvas and moves the pattern onto it. Zarougui said that it was not easy to learn the style. She spent many years in another country to study Ebru, and she got a degree in it. The woman had to leave her home because it was not possible to study Ebru in Tunisia. Difficult words: dye (a substance which changes the color of clothes, hair, and so on), pattern repeated shapes, colors, or lines that are usually for decoration), canvas (a piece of cloth which artists use for painting). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Difficult words: oily (something that feels like water, but it is thicker and smoother), dye (a substance which changes the color of hair, clothes, or other things), pattern (shapes, colors, and lines which repeat and make a picture). Dr. Jane Goodall, the world-renowned primatologist, conservationist , and animal rights advocate, has passed away at the age of 91. According to the Jane Goodall Institute, she died of natural causes in California while on a speaking tour in the United States. Goodall revolutionised the scientific understanding of wild chimpanzees and their behavior. Her work not only transformed primate research but also deepened our knowledge of human evolution. She began her studies in Africa at the age of 26, despite having no formal scientific education, and gained the trust of chimpanzees through patience and empathy. Her lifelong mission was to protect nature and inspire global action for the planet. Even in her final days, she remained active, recently giving interviews and public talks. Jane Goodall’s legacy continues through her institute and her message of hope for a sustainable world. Difficult words: primatologist (a scientist who studies monkeys and apes), conservationist (a person who works to protect nature, animals, and the environment), revolutionise (to completely change something in a big and important way). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Her research helped people understand chimpanzees and also humans. Goodall worked all her life to protect animals and nature. She often spoke about hope and caring for the Earth. Before her death, she gave interviews and talks in the US. Her institute continues her mission of protecting the planet. Difficult words: natural cause (when someone dies because of illness or age, not by accident or violence), education (studying at school), institute (an organization that does research or education about a special subject). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Difficult words: act (to do something), tour (a trip to different places, often to speak or show something), brave (not afraid). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A family in East Vancouver, Canada, experienced a truly unexpected and unforgettable moment when Grammy-winning R&B artist Daniel Caesar came to their home. They were spending a normal afternoon in their backyard when a polite man appeared at their gate. He kindly asked if his friend could use their bathroom. To their surprise, that friend was Daniel Caesar himself. The singer entered the house with his videographer , introduced himself warmly, and accepted a glass of water. He spent about fifteen minutes chatting with the family and their children about his tour, his music, and his family life. Caesar showed genuine interest in the kids, asking them questions and making them laugh. The parents later told their children that meeting such a famous person at home would never happen again. They described Daniel Caesar as humble, gracious , and very down-to-earth. Difficult words: videographer (a person who films videos professionally), genuine (real, honest), gracious (kind and polite in behavior). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Two decades ago, Europe’s bluefin tuna was close to collapse due to overfishing driven by the global sushi market. Industrial fleets operated with little oversight , and illegal catches were widespread. Scientists warned of the crisis, and activists demanded urgent action. In 2007, the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) introduced a strict recovery plan, supported by the European Union. It included quotas , smaller fleets, shorter fishing seasons, and international inspections. This reduced catches dramatically, allowing tuna stocks to recover faster than expected. Today, fishing is tightly controlled. In France, every tuna must be weighed, labelled, and tracked. Fisher cooperatives support the system because it ensures long-term sustainability. Scientists continue to monitor populations through tagging and aerial surveys, which have shown remarkable growth in tuna schools. However, experts warn that illegal fishing could return. The recovery is strong, but its future depends on strict control and continued cooperation between scientists, industry, and governments. Difficult words: fleet (a group of ships, usually used for fishing, the navy, or transport), oversight (careful control), quota (fixed amount allowed). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Twenty years ago, bluefin tuna in Europe was in danger. Too many boats caught too many fish because sushi became very popular worldwide. There were no real rules, and illegal fishing was everywhere. Scientists warned, and activists asked governments to act . In 2007, a recovery plan started. It set quotas , reduced the number of fishing boats, and created inspections. This reduced catches and helped tuna grow again. Now, fishing is under strong control. In France, fishers weigh and label every tuna. They support the rules because they protect the future of the industry. Scientists also use tagging and flights over the sea to check the number of tuna. Experts say the future is positive but warn against illegal fishing. Difficult words: act (to do something), recovery (the process of getting better or becoming strong again after problems), quota (the amount of something you can do). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Difficult words: disappear (to no longer exist), quota (the number of something which you can do), label (to put information on something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
